questions.question: The height of a binary tree is the number of edges in the longest path from the root to a leaf in the tree. The maximum possible height of a full binary tree with [latex]23[/latex] nodes is ________.(answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
In a full binary tree, every node has either [latex]0[/latex] or [latex]2[/latex] children. If there are [latex]I[/latex] internal (2-children) nodes and [latex]L[/latex] leaves, then [latex]L=I+1[/latex], and total nodes [latex]N=I+L=2I+1[/latex].

For [latex]N=23[/latex]: [latex]23=2I+1\Rightarrow I=11[/latex] internal nodes and [latex]L=12[/latex] leaves.

To maximize height, make the tree as "skewed"/chain-like as possible while still keeping every internal node's 2-children rule: each internal node (except the last one in the chain) has one leaf child and one internal child continuing the chain; the very last internal node has two leaf children.

This chain uses exactly [latex]I=11[/latex] internal nodes along the main path, with the deepest leaves appearing right after the [latex]11[/latex]th internal node. So the longest root-to-leaf path has [latex]11[/latex] edges.

Answer: 11

questions.question:
The set [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] represents various traversals over binary tree. The set [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] represents the order of visiting nodes during a traversal.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \quad\quad\textbf{T} & \quad\quad\quad\textbf{S} \\ \hline \text{I: Inorder} & \text{L: left subtree, node, right subtree} \\ \text{II: Preorder} & \text{M: node, left subtree, right subtree} \\ \text{III: Postorder} & \text{N: left subtree, right subtree, node} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following is the correct match from [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] ?
questions.explanation:
Recall the definitions of each traversal (in terms of the order root/current node is visited relative to its subtrees):

- Inorder (I): visit left subtree, then the node itself, then right subtree — this matches L (left subtree, node, right subtree).
- Preorder (II): visit the node itself first, then left subtree, then right subtree — this matches M (node, left subtree, right subtree).
- Postorder (III): visit left subtree, then right subtree, and the node itself last — this matches N (left subtree, right subtree, node).

Answer: I-L, II-M, III-N

Click here for detail solution

questions.question:
Let [latex]n[/latex] be an odd number greater than [latex]100[/latex]. Consider a binary minheap with [latex]n[/latex] elements stored in an array [latex]P[/latex] whose index starts from [latex]1[/latex].
Which of the following indices of [latex]P[/latex] do/does NOT correspond to any leaf node of the minheap?
questions.explanation:
In a 1-indexed array representation of a binary heap with [latex]n[/latex] elements, the leaf nodes are exactly the indices [latex]\left\lfloor \dfrac{n}{2}\right\rfloor+1[/latex] through [latex]n[/latex] (nodes with no children).

For odd [latex]n[/latex], [latex]\left\lfloor n/2\right\rfloor=\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex], so:
- Leaf indices: [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}+1=\dfrac{n+1}{2}[/latex] up to [latex]n[/latex].
- Internal (non-leaf) indices: [latex]1[/latex] up to [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex].

Checking the given indices:
- [latex]\dfrac{n+1}{2}[/latex]: this is the first leaf index — corresponds to a leaf.
- [latex]n[/latex]: this is the last leaf — corresponds to a leaf.
- [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex]: this is the last internal node index — it does NOT correspond to a leaf.
- [latex]\dfrac{n-3}{2}[/latex]: this is less than [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex], so also an internal node — does NOT correspond to a leaf.

Answer: indices (n-1)/2 and (n-3)/2 do NOT correspond to leaf nodes.

We want a recursive count of nodes in a non-empty singly linked list.

The natural recursive base case is: if the current node is the last node (i.e. [latex]\text{head->next==NULL}[/latex]), then this contributes exactly [latex]1[/latex] to the count, so [latex]\text{E1: head->next==NULL}[/latex], returning [latex]1[/latex].

Otherwise, the count is [latex]1[/latex] (for the current node) plus however many nodes remain in the rest of the list starting from [latex]\text{head->next}[/latex]: [latex]\text{E2: 1+getListSize(head->next)}[/latex].

(Using [latex]\text{head==NULL}[/latex] as the base case instead would also work logically for a possibly-empty list, but here the function is documented to be called only on a non-empty list, and combined with the given E2 form, the option that consistently checks [latex]\text{head->next}[/latex] in the base case and recurses on [latex]\text{head->next}[/latex] is the matching, correct pair.)

Answer: E1: head->next == NULL, E2: 1 + getListSize(head->next)

questions.question:
You are given a set [latex]V[/latex] of distinct integers. A binary search tree [latex]T[/latex] is created by inserting all elements of [latex]V[/latex] one by one, starting with an empty tree. The tree [latex]T[/latex] follows the convention that, at each node, all values stored in the left subtree of the node are smaller than the value stored at the node. You are not aware of the sequence in which these values were inserted into [latex]T[/latex], and you do not have access to [latex]T[/latex].
Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: Inorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]
options.B: Root node of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]
options.C: Preorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]
options.D: Postorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]

questions.explanation:
The inorder traversal of any BST is the keys in sorted order, whatever the insertion order. So it can be found from V just by sorting.

Root, preorder and postorder depend on the insertion order. Example V = {1, 2}: inserting 1 then 2 gives root 1; inserting 2 then 1 gives root 2.

Answer: Inorder traversal of T can be determined from V

questions.question:
In a double hashing scheme, [latex] h_1(k) = k \mod 11 [/latex] and [latex] h_2(k) = 1 + (k \mod 7) [/latex] are the auxiliary hash functions. The size [latex] m [/latex] of the hash table is 11. The hash function for the [latex] i [/latex]-th probe in the open address table is [latex] [h_1(k) + i h_2(k)] \mod m [/latex] The following keys are inserted in the given order: 63, 50, 25, 79, 67, 24.

The slot at which key 24 gets stored is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
Double hashing: [latex]h_1(k)=k\bmod11[/latex], [latex]h_2(k)=1+(k\bmod7)[/latex], probe [latex]i[/latex]: [latex][h_1(k)+ih_2(k)]\bmod11[/latex], table size [latex]11[/latex].

Insert in order, computing initial slot (and probing forward on collision):
[latex]63[/latex]: [latex]h_1=8[/latex] → slot [latex]8[/latex] (empty).
[latex]50[/latex]: [latex]h_1=6[/latex] → slot [latex]6[/latex] (empty).
[latex]25[/latex]: [latex]h_1=3[/latex] → slot [latex]3[/latex] (empty).
[latex]79[/latex]: [latex]h_1=2[/latex] → slot [latex]2[/latex] (empty).
[latex]67[/latex]: [latex]h_1=1[/latex] → slot [latex]1[/latex] (empty).
[latex]24[/latex]: [latex]h_1=2[/latex] (taken by [latex]79[/latex]), [latex]h_2=1+(24\bmod7)=1+3=4[/latex]. Probe [latex]i=1[/latex]: [latex](2+4)\bmod11=6[/latex] (taken by [latex]50[/latex]). Probe [latex]i=2[/latex]: [latex](2+8)\bmod11=10[/latex] (empty) → placed at slot [latex]10[/latex].

Answer: 10
